title: Title, date and speaker
short: A dramatic monologue from Men and Women (1855). An Englishman playing an old Venetian keyboard piece speaks to its dead composer, Baldassare Galuppi.
body: The archive's 'Dramatic Lyrics (1842)' label is mistaken. The poem first appeared in Men and Women (1855), vol. 1, and was probably written between 1847 and 1853, while the Brownings lived in Italy. A toccata (Italian toccare, 'to touch') is a keyboard piece meant to display the player's touch. Baldassare Galuppi (1706–85) was a Venetian composer, known for comic operas and as maestro di cappella of St Mark's. The speaker is a nineteenth-century English amateur of science. He addresses Galuppi as if the music were the composer's voice and finds its 'meaning' hard to bear ('very sad to find'). The monologue blends social satire of eighteenth-century Venice with the speaker's own unease.

title: Which piece?
short: No particular Galuppi toccata has been identified. Browning owned manuscript volumes of Galuppi's 'toccata-pieces' but may have had no single work in mind.
body: In 1887 Browning noted that he owned two manuscript volumes of Galuppi's toccata-pieces, so he knew the music directly. Scholars have not been able to match the poem's harmonic details to any surviving piece. In Galuppi's time 'toccata' and 'sonata' were used loosely for keyboard works, and several sonatas have been proposed. The general view is that Browning combined typical features of the style. A minority of musicologists have tried to show that the poem's own structure imitates a musical form.

anchor: this is very sad to find
title: Metre and stanza
short: Fifteen monorhymed tercets in long trochaic lines of eight stresses, usually ending on a stressed syllable. The rhythm suggests the steady pulse of keyboard figuration.
body: Each three-line stanza holds a single rhyme (find / blind / mind; brings / kings / rings). The lines are trochaic octameter, usually catalectic (the last unstressed syllable dropped), so each ends firmly on a stress. The archive breaks a few long lines in two to fit the page. The insistent, regular beat and the rhyme repeated three times give a mechanical, pattering motion, often compared to a toccata's busy keyboard figures. It also lets Browning slide easily between dialogue, description and reflection.

title: Wedding the sea
short: The Doge's ceremony of 'marrying' the Adriatic: every Ascension Day he cast a ring into the sea to signify Venice's maritime dominion.
body: In the Sposalizio del Mare, celebrated on Ascension Day, the Doge sailed out in the state barge, the Bucintoro, and dropped a gold ring into the Adriatic, declaring the city's marriage to the sea. 'Where the merchants were the kings' alludes to Venice as a mercantile republic ruled by an oligarchy of merchant families. The Republic ended in 1797, about a decade after Galuppi's death, which gives the speaker's picture of a pleasure-loving city a sense of approaching doom.

anchor: Shylock's bridge with houses on it
title: Shylock's bridge
short: The Rialto bridge, lined with shops, named here from Shylock's 'In the Rialto' in The Merchant of Venice.
body: The speaker cannot recall the name of the bridge ('what you call') and identifies it through Shakespeare, as an untravelled Englishman would. The Rialto bridge over the Grand Canal carries rows of shops, hence 'with houses on it'. In The Merchant of Venice Shylock speaks of being berated 'In the Rialto' (1.3), meaning the exchange district. The line 'I was never out of England' that follows makes the joke explicit. The whole Venice of the poem is put together from literature and music.

anchor: I was never out of England
title: Imagined Venice
short: The speaker admits he has never been abroad: his vivid Venice is an imaginative reconstruction prompted by the music.
body: The admission ironically undercuts the speaker's authority. The scenes that follow, balls, masks, flirtation, are what he imagines the music 'says', not historical knowledge. The poem thus examines how music calls up meaning. It is a drama of the listener's projection as much as of the composer's art. Browning, who lived in Italy, writes ironically about a provincial Englishman, but also with sympathy, since the speaker's response to the music is real.

anchor: Balls and masks begun at midnight
title: Carnival
short: The masked balls of the Venetian carnival, famous in the eighteenth century for pleasure and licence.
body: Eighteenth-century Venice was known across Europe for its long carnival season, in which masks allowed anonymity and freedom across classes. The festivities lasting from 'midnight' to 'mid-day', and the 'fresh adventures for the morrow', compress that reputation for pleasure and intrigue. The lady 'bite[s] her mask's black velvet' in stanza 6, a detail of the moretta or black velvet mask. The speaker's questions ('do you say?') show him reading all this into the music.

anchor: like a bell-flower on its bed
title: The lady
short: A fleshly portrait of a Venetian beauty: the small face 'buoyant' on the neck like a bell-flower, over an abundant bosom.
body: The fifth stanza makes the music into a woman's body. The round cheeks and red lips, the small face bobbing like a campanula on its stem, and 'the breast's superb abundance where a man might base his head' are sensuous and slightly comic in their frankness. 'Base' here means rest or lay down. In a poem full of musical terms the word may also hint at the musical bass, though this is only a possibility. The portrait prepares the ending, where 'Dear dead women' with golden hair become the poem's central image of mortality.

title: clavichord
short: A quiet keyboard instrument in which brass tangents strike the strings. The lovers barely pause their flirtation as Galuppi plays.
body: The clavichord was a small domestic keyboard instrument, very soft in tone, in which metal tangents strike the strings. It suits the poem's intimate scene, though Galuppi's public music would more often have been played on the harpsichord. The picture is ironic. The composer sits 'stately' while the lovers break off talk only for a moment, she to bite her mask, he to finger his sword (a hint of duels and intrigue). The music is a background to pleasure.

title: Lesser thirds, diminished sixths, suspensions, solutions
short: Technical harmony: minor ('lesser') thirds, diminished sixths, suspensions (notes held over into the next chord) and their resolutions ('solutions').
body: The speaker now 'reads' the music's harmony as speech. 'Lesser thirds' are minor thirds, traditionally heard as plaintive. 'Sixths diminished' are dissonant intervals that sound like a sigh. 'Suspensions' are notes held over from one chord into the next, which produce tension, and 'solutions' are their resolutions (an older term). 'Commiserating sevenths' are seventh chords, dissonances that call for resolution. Each device is given a voice: 'Must we die?', 'Life might last! we can but try!' Browning was musically trained, and the technical language is accurate, but the 'translations' are the speaker's own.

title: The dominant's persistence
short: A chord on the dominant (fifth) note of the key insists until it must resolve to the tonic. The 'octave' answers it.
body: In tonal harmony the dominant (the fifth degree of the scale), especially as a dominant seventh, creates the strongest expectation of return to the tonic, the home key. The 'persistence' that 'must be answered to' is a sustained or repeated dominant. The answer, 'an octave struck', is the final resolution. In stanza 8 the musical tension is turned into the lovers' dialogue of kisses ('a million seemed so few'), and the cadence falls like a conversation's end. The music's resolution is also an image of death, which is the answer to every life.

title: tacitly
short: Death arrives silently (Latin tacitus, 'silent'), with a musical overtone: when the music stops, death enters.
body: 'Tacitly' means silently, unspoken, from Latin tacere ('to be silent'). The word is unexpectedly Latinate in a line of monosyllables. It may also suggest the musical direction 'tacet' ('it is silent'), by which a part falls silent, the music stopping as the lives end. The stanza's summary of the Venetians, 'Some with lives that came to nothing, some with deeds as well undone', is moral judgement given almost casually. The phrase 'where they never see the sun' recalls classical and biblical pictures of the dark underworld.

title: The speaker's science
short: The speaker is a Victorian amateur of science, physics, geology, mathematics, confident in his reason until the 'cold music' unsettles him.
body: When the speaker sits down 'to reason' and triumphs over 'a secret wrung from nature's close reserve', he speaks for nineteenth-century scientific confidence. The music's ghostly voice later mocks his learning: 'you know physics, something of geology, / Mathematics are your pastime'. The irony is aimed at a faith in intellect as a guarantee of the soul's worth. Geology in particular (Lyell's Principles of Geology, 1830–33) had unsettled traditional ideas of time and creation in the decades before the poem.

title: Ghostly cricket
short: The music sounds like a cricket chirping in the ruins of a burned house: thin, persistent and mournful.
body: The simile 'like a ghostly cricket, creaking where a house was burned' gives the harpsichord-like tinkle of the old music an eerie quality. It is a small dry sound surviving among ruins. Folklore treated the cricket on the hearth as a domestic spirit (as in Dickens's The Cricket on the Hearth, 1845), and here the hearth is gone. The image suits the poem's view of eighteenth-century Venice as a civilisation burned out and remembered only through its music.

anchor: Dust and ashes, dead and done
title: Dust and ashes
short: This is a biblical formula of human mortality and humility (Genesis 18:27; Job 30:19, 42:6), which the music 'creaks' as its refrain.
body: Abraham calls himself 'but dust and ashes' (Genesis 18:27), and Job says 'I am become like dust and ashes' (Job 30:19) and repents 'in dust and ashes' (42:6). In the poem the phrase is put into the music's mouth as a sardonic verdict: 'Venice spent what Venice earned'. It returns at the start of the last stanza as 'So you creak it'. The repetition gives the moralising its shape, in which a pleasure-loving society reaps the consequences. The speaker cannot answer it ('I want the heart to scold', meaning he lacks the heart).

anchor: where a soul can be discerned
title: The soul, doubtless, is immortal
short: The music's sardonic qualification: the soul is immortal only 'where a soul can be discerned', perhaps in the earnest scientist, not in the merry Venetians.
body: This is one of the poem's main cruxes. The ghostly voice grants immortality only to those who have souls worth the name. Read straight, the scientist's serious mind will survive ('you'll not die, it cannot be!'), while the Venetians, 'merely born to bloom and drop', had nothing left 'when the kissing had to stop'. Most critics take the lines ironically. The music mocks the speaker's assumption that intellect earns immortality, and his final chill shows that he has felt the mockery. The poem never settles whether Browning endorses any part of the judgement.

title: Butterflies and extinction
short: The butterfly is the ancient emblem of the soul (Greek psyche), and 'extinction' carries the new geological sense of species dying out.
body: In Greek psyche means both 'soul' and 'butterfly', and the butterfly emerging from its chrysalis was a traditional emblem of the soul's resurrection. Here the butterflies stand for the frivolous Venetians, who 'may dread extinction'. The word has a pointed modern meaning, since pre-Darwinian geology had made the extinction of species a public topic (Chambers's Vestiges, 1844). The speaker is mockingly assured that he, unlike the butterflies, cannot die. The irony works because his science is the very thing that made extinction thinkable.

anchor: Dear dead women, with such hair
title: Dear dead women
short: The famous close: the speaker's thoughts turn from argument to the dead women's golden hair, and he feels 'chilly and grown old'.
body: The last stanza moves from the music's moralising to a wistful, physical image. The hair that 'Used to hang and brush their bosoms' recalls the lady of stanza 5. Critics have read the ending in several ways. In one reading it is genuine elegy, the speaker mourning the lost beauty he had dismissed. In another it is self-revelation, his complacent superiority dissolving into a sense of his own ageing and mortality. In a third, Browning gives the last word to sensuous life over abstract argument. 'I feel chilly and grown old' brings the 'cold music' of stanza 11 into the speaker's own body.
